editions.title: Microsoft quits Nscale site as AI trade wobbles and iPhone Duo supply strains
editions.intro:
The biggest story is a reported setback for Nscale, the British AI cloud startup. The Telegraph reports that Microsoft has pulled out of a deal to anchor Nscale's first UK data centre in Loughton, Essex, weeks before Nscale's planned IPO of up to $3bn. Nscale says it remains committed to the site and that its Microsoft relationship is strong, and Microsoft has not commented. The report lands as investors grow wary of neocloud firms, and CoreWeave shares were marked down in coverage of the story.

The wider backdrop is a deepening selloff in US tech shares. Bloomberg reports that this is exposing weak spots in Asia's AI "picks and shovels" suppliers, with rising financing costs threatening data-centre and hardware spending. The FT also argues that America's roughly $10tn AI infrastructure build-out is running into physical constraints. Against that, SemiAnalysis says more than 300 local data-centre moratoriums have delayed only a few projects so far. Meta's earnings, previewed by the FT as a test of confidence in AI spending, are the next major read-across.

Apple dominated the rest of the day's flow. The iPhone Duo, its first foldable, is reportedly sold out into January, with staff told walk-in buyers are unlikely to get stock on launch day, and Gurman calls the staggered pre-order rollout a "major mistake". Apple's EU energy label put the device's battery at 4,883 mAh. Rumours also point to a touchscreen MacBook and a HomeView smart display with a robotic arm, with a possible retail refresh on 6 November. Most of these remain unconfirmed.

top_stories.summary: Apple Store staff reportedly told customers without pre-orders to expect no launch-day stock. Apple says demand is extraordinary, and shipping estimates have slipped to around late January in most countries.

editions.title: Microsoft Walks Away From Nscale Site as Neocloud Nerves Grow
editions.intro:
The biggest story of the day is Microsoft's reported withdrawal from an anchor deal for Nscale's first British data centre in Loughton, Essex. The Telegraph says Microsoft has pulled out weeks before the AI cloud startup's planned IPO, which is reported to seek up to $3bn. Nscale says it remains committed to the site and that its Microsoft relationship is strong, while Microsoft has not commented. Grid connection delays at the site were also reported, and the story is being read as a sign of wider caution toward neocloud firms.

That caution fed into a broader theme of AI-trade nerves. Bloomberg reports that a deepening selloff in US tech shares is exposing weak spots in Asia's AI supply chain, with rising financing costs threatening data-centre and hardware spending. The Financial Times, meanwhile, argues America's roughly $10tn AI infrastructure build-out is running into physical limits of power, equipment and money. Investors will look to Meta's earnings next, which the FT frames as a test of whether confidence in the AI spending boom can be restored.

Elsewhere, Ericsson beat expectations with third-quarter adjusted EBITA of SEK 10.1bn against a consensus of SEK 7.93bn, and its shares rose as much as 11% in Stockholm. On the chip front, a single unverified report says Nvidia wants Samsung, Micron and SK hynix to build custom HBM base dies on TSMC's 3nm process, while a separate rumour suggests China could let major firms buy H200 chips under tight caps. Both remain unconfirmed.

editions.title: Nvidia RTX 5090 Row, TSMC Profit Record and Starlink Limits Dominate
editions.intro: TSMC posted a record quarterly profit, with demand for AI chips still far outstripping supply, but it signalled caution on 2027. Meanwhile, the AI trade showed strain: Asian chip suppliers were exposed to a US tech selloff, and reports that OpenAI's revenue trails expectations added to nerves. Ukraine's dispute with SpaceX over Starlink speed limits escalated, with Zelenskyy calling the restrictions deliberate. Apple's iPhone Duo faced shortages and Apple's chief executive called memory supply a crisis.

top_stories.title: TSMC records sixth straight record profit, cautious on 2027
top_stories.summary: TSMC reported record third-quarter net profit of NT$763.1bn, up 69%, with revenue up 51%. It guided to about 44% dollar revenue growth in 2026, but chairman C.C. Wei warned that price-sensitive consumer markets are under pressure and that the company is being prudent about 2027.

top_stories.title: Starshield speed limits cut Ukrainian interceptor drones
top_stories.summary: Speed limits on SpaceX's Starshield network reportedly cut links for interceptor drones above about 161 km/h, forcing Ukrainian units to cancel missions. Reports suggest the order came from the White House or was discussed by Musk and Trump, but these claims are unverified.

top_stories.title: Apple's Ternus calls memory shortage a crisis
top_stories.summary: Apple's chief executive told TIME that memory chip constraints are a crisis and all options should be considered. The comments follow a report that Apple tested memory chips from a Chinese firm, which prompted US warnings against them.

top_stories.title: Microsoft plans multi-gigawatt Maia 300 rollout
top_stories.summary: Microsoft plans to scale its Maia accelerators to multi-gigawatt deployments from 2027, with Maia 300 as its primary inference system. Analysts expect Maia to be only about 10% of its AI chip spend by early 2027, so Nvidia's position is not yet under threat.

top_stories.title: Intel confirms Razor Lake-AX timing and 700 TOPS target
top_stories.summary: Intel SVP Cho Min-sung confirmed Nova Lake for 2027 and Razor Lake-AX for 2028, the latter targeting 700 TOPS of AI compute. The aim is premium devices and physical AI.

top_stories.title: Tesla shows fan-powered Roadster, production 2028
top_stories.summary: Tesla demonstrated its next-generation Roadster using powered fans and a retractable rear wing for downforce. Musk said production begins in 2028, with reservations open at $50,000 for the base model and $250,000 for the Thrust trim.

rumour_watch.note: A reported $20bn revenue shortfall at OpenAI, relayed without a named source. Plausible given the market backdrop, but it is an internal figure and OpenAI has not confirmed it.
Nvidia's Jeff Fisher reportedly denied the RTX 5090 is discontinued, citing tight supply. Credible on the record, but retailer listings at inflated prices suggest supply is genuinely thin.
Reported FTC demands aimed at OpenAI and Anthropic. Only a feed summary, and the story stresses it is not a finding of wrongdoing, so treat as unconfirmed.
DeepSeek says its new Flash model beats larger rivals on agentic tasks. Weights are public, but independent benchmarks are still pending.

Anduril opens a $1.3bn employee tender at a $90bn valuation, up from $61bn in May.
Berkshire Hathaway buys a further $330m of Bending Spoons shares, lifting its stake to about 4%.
Netflix names Peter Rice chief content officer as Bela Bajaria leaves, a day after a 6% staff cut.
Meta removes contested scraping language from its commercial terms after criticism from publishers and experts.

Finance.title: AI selloff spreads to Asia as yields and oil climb
Finance.summary:
The dominant theme is a sharp reversal in AI-linked equities. US chip stocks had an eight-session rout, the longest since 2008, and the Philadelphia semiconductor index fell about 16 percent. The selloff has spread to Asia's AI supply chain, with a Goldman basket of regional AI hardware names down 11 percent last week. Investors fear that rising borrowing costs could curb the data-centre spending behind the rally, and that financing strain at hyperscalers and neoclouds such as CoreWeave could reduce chip orders. Some investors still see demand as strong. Related market signals include the 10-year Treasury yield moving above 5% for the first time in almost two decades, a rise in the VIX, and US stocks falling on Friday.

Energy and geopolitics are adding to the pressure. Oil rose to around US$110 a barrel as Iran-related tensions in the Strait of Hormuz persisted, and Iran says it is reviewing a US response to a proposal to end its eight-month war. In the Middle East, fighting between Saudi-led forces and Houthis in Yemen has escalated, and Egypt has moved to support Saudi Arabia. Russia says its first tanker carrying Russian oil to world markets has left Dikson, and it argues the market faces a shortfall of 4-6 million barrels a day.

Elsewhere, the Starlink dispute is dominating transatlantic and Ukraine coverage. The US has reportedly threatened Europe over Starlink restrictions, Treasury Secretary Bessent called Zelenskyy's accusation over slower Starlink service in Ukraine 'reckless', and Zelenskiy says US intelligence-sharing has resumed. In Europe, Paris and other French cities saw riots over high prices, with Carrefour reporting around 50 stores ransacked. In the UK, GDP unexpectedly rose and markets are debating a possible Bank of England rate rise in November.

points.text: Michael Burry warns 55% of S&P 500 stocks were in bear markets on 6 October, comparing the setup with March 2000.
The VIX rose 21.5% to 19.99 on Friday, its biggest one-day jump since June 5, as the S&P 500 fell 1.09%.
Indonesian stocks had their worst day since 1998 after MSCI warned it could downgrade the market.
Carrefour says around 50 stores and almost 20 supermarkets were ransacked during riots across France.
Bloomberg argues UK inflation data could decide whether the BoE delivers a November rate hike.
Bessent called Zelenskyy's Starlink accusation 'reckless', highlighting strains over US support for Kyiv.

World.title: France unrest, Russia-Ukraine energy strikes dominate world news
World.summary:
The most significant story today is the wave of violent protests across France over the cost of living and school conditions. Reports describe riots, looting and fires, with about 1,800 to over 2,000 arrests, around 1,500 businesses damaged and the historic Limoges town hall largely destroyed. Interior Ministry attendance figures of 550,000 contrast with the CGT's 800,000. Ministers held crisis talks, opposition politicians have called for the interior minister to resign, and Emmanuel Macron was due to address the nation. With presidential elections about six months away, the political fallout is likely to intensify, and French equities have fallen.

Unrest has spread beyond France, with housing and living-cost protests reported in Milan, Lisbon and Albania. Albania's Tirana has seen six days of clashes calling for Prime Minister Edi Rama to resign. Separately, the Russia-Ukraine energy war has escalated. Ukraine launched more than 1,000 drones, striking oil terminals and depots in St Petersburg, while Moscow airports briefly closed. Oil prices rose on the attacks, and the US waiver of sweeping Russia sanctions for 60 days has drawn bipartisan criticism.

Middle East tensions also feature: Egypt pledged support for Saudi Arabia after Houthi attacks, Israeli settler violence against European diplomats in the West Bank has drawn EU condemnation ahead of the 27 October Israeli election, and Trump has endorsed Netanyahu. Markets should watch oil, the euro and French assets for signs of political instability.

points.text: Politicians from left and right have called for the French interior minister, Laurent Nuñez, to resign after the unrest.
Russia and Ukraine continue hitting each other's energy infrastructure after Trump's announced energy ceasefire broke down.
Rubio said the US waiver of Russia sanctions lasts 60 days, during which the administration will assess economic effects.
Albania's PM Edi Rama refuses to resign after six days of protests, with 272 injured including 169 police officers.
The EU condemned an attack by Israeli settlers on European diplomats in the occupied West Bank and demanded accountability.
Drone attacks on Black Sea shipping have intensified, with a tanker set ablaze off Romania's coast and seven crew missing.

Tech.title: Microsoft pulls out of Nscale UK site before IPO
Tech.summary:
The biggest story in tech today is the report that Microsoft has pulled out of a deal to anchor Nscale's first British data centre in Loughton, Essex. The timing is awkward for Nscale, an AI cloud startup preparing an IPO seeking up to $3bn. Nscale says it remains committed to the site and that its Microsoft relationship is strong, while Microsoft has not commented. The site has also faced grid connection delays, and the story is being read alongside wider investor caution about neocloud firms, which weighs on the sector.

That caution fits a broader worry about the AI trade. Bloomberg reports a deepening selloff in US tech shares is exposing weak spots in Asia's AI rally, as rising financing costs could curb the data-centre and hardware spending that has powered suppliers. The FT asks whether Meta's earnings can restore confidence in AI investment, and separately argues that America's roughly $10tn AI infrastructure build-out is running into physical limits. SemiAnalysis, however, finds that more than 300 local data centre moratoriums have delayed only a few projects so far.

Elsewhere, Apple dominates the news flow, with the iPhone Duo's launch and pre-order problems, a reported cut to iPhone 18 Pro orders, and a range of rumoured products. Nvidia and Samsung are also in the news over custom memory and chip sourcing, and Samsung's Galaxy chip choice is in question. Most of these items are unverified reports, so they should be treated with care.

points.text: A report says Apple has cut iPhone 18 Pro orders by up to 20%, but it is unsourced and unverified.
Gurman says Apple made a major mistake by opening iPhone Duo pre-orders in over 70 countries at once.

Reports suggest China may let Alibaba, ByteDance and DeepSeek buy Nvidia H200 chips, with tight supply caps.
Disney agreed to hire at least 60 Character.AI staff after the chatbot startup filed for bankruptcy.
Anthropic is consulting law firms on fair negotiation norms for AI agents that may soon strike deals.

Fashion.title: Luxury houses expand in China as creative roles shift
Fashion.summary:
The biggest story is Chanel's plan to open its first Wuhan boutique at the SKP department store, a move that comes as luxury brands in China work through a prolonged market reset. The store will sit on SKP's K Avenue alongside Louis Vuitton and Cartier, and Celine, Giorgio Armani and Prada are also set to open there, timed with the WWD x SKP Global Fashion & Beauty Summit. The expansion sits against a backdrop of brands closing weaker stores and testing new regional markets.

Creative leadership is also in flux. Seán McGirr is leaving Alexander McQueen after three years, with his Spring/Summer 2027 London show as his final collection. He follows Sarah Burton, who moved to Givenchy, and no successor has been named. Separately, Vogue Scandinavia reports that Veronica Leoni is leaving Calvin Klein after four seasons, though the item gives no detail on reasons or a replacement.

Elsewhere, the sector's mood looks less buoyant. Business of Fashion headlines point to weak numbers, empty chairs and a possible slowdown in US demand for luxury goods, though the details are not available in the feed. Jewellery and watches remain strong draws: Cartier unveiled 46 new high jewellery pieces in Kyoto, and a limited Biver AB watch sold out before images were released. Victoria's Secret's Pink, meanwhile, is taking the halftime slot at its show, with Rosie Huntington-Whiteley returning to the runway.

points.text: Business of Fashion describes weak luxury numbers and leadership vacancies, though the companies involved are not named in the feed.

A $82,000 Biver AB watch sold out through a retailer's fan group chat before images were shared, with sold-out until 2029.
Pink takes the halftime slot at the Victoria's Secret show, citing five straight quarters of growth and a refocus on 18 to 24-year-olds.
Rosie Huntington-Whiteley returns to the Victoria's Secret runway 16 years after leaving in 2010.
